highlights: GT3 combines rotary mowing, vacuuming and clipping/debris collection with automatic hopper emptying and task resumption.
The 914.4 mm cutting width belongs to GT3; its manufacturer-rated area per full charge is 20000 m², not an hourly cleaning rate.
Disabling the blades enables sweeping; border mapping, edited no-go areas and mapped inter-zone transit support site configuration.
Robot mass includes batteries. Two-hour charging requires the optional 6 kW fast charger rather than the standard 3 kW charger.
GT5 uses a 1.52 m rotary cutting deck with clipping collection, automatic hopper emptying and mapped cross-zone travel.
Manufacturer gives 850 kg including batteries, 8-10 h runtime and a 20° maximum mowing slope; these are not GT7 reel-mower specifications.
RGB/RGBD/LiDAR sensing and drop-off detection support navigation; the page safety language is not an independent collision-prevention guarantee.
The 4 h charging figure requires the optional 6 kW fast charger; standard 3 kW charging is 8 h.
GT7 uses three floating reel cutting units, four-wheel drive and RTK/LiDAR/vision positioning, separate from GT3/GT5 rotary mowers.
Eight- or eleven-blade reels and 5-50 mm cutting height are manufacturer configurations; working and lifted widths differ.
The advertised 12 h duration and 7 ha per charge apply to non-collection mode; active grass collection is a different operating mode.
Standard 3 kW charging is 8 h; 4 h requires optional 6 kW equipment. IP66 from GT3/GT5 is not inherited by GT7.
Configurable cutting angles, directional rotation and lane offsets support turf patterns; four-wheel drive and independently floating cutting units support contour following.
C55 sweeps and scrubs in one pass using a triple-roller arrangement; it is positioned for medium/large facilities and heavy floor soil.
Dual battery compartments permit a claimed five-second hot swap while powered on. The listed five-hour runtime and four-hour charging time remain separate from staffed battery-exchange operation.
Maximum theoretical output is 2376 m²/h with 550 mm scrubbing width excluding side brushes; this is not measured facility productivity.
The water-tank table gives 60 L clean plus 47 L waste, while the headline says 110 L. That unresolved capacity difference remains explicit instead of treating 110 L as usable clean water.
Top-mounted LiDAR and four stereo-vision sensors support navigation; the page claims speed-bump crossing up to 5 cm, which is not a general stair/vertical-step capability.

A building-connected workstation enables automatic charging, water supply and drainage. Manual assist handling and a claimed three-second tank flip support maintenance; integration and included hardware require confirmation.

App/web dispatch, cleaning reports, interruption resumption, elevator/gate connections and mixed-robot collaboration are manufacturer-described workflows; thirty-second drying is not a slip-safety guarantee.
C20 combines sweeping, vacuuming and mopping in a roughly 35 cm-high modular body for low-clearance hard-floor maintenance.
Cleaning width depends on the task: 450 mm for sweeping/vacuuming and 285 mm for scrubbing; machine mass includes the battery and empty water tanks.
Separate 7 L clean-water and 5 L wastewater tanks avoid reusing dirty water; tank volume is not rated cargo payload.
Removable sweeping/vacuum, dust-bin, rear-mop and side-brush modules support maintenance. App/web tools cover remote dispatch, status and cleaning reports.
T11 combines five stereo-vision sensors with VSLAM for manufacturer-rated passage through 49 cm aisles.
A six-wheel shock-absorbing chassis and motion-control system support stable service in narrow spaces; advertising display and customizable interaction support customer engagement.
The listed 20 kg total capacity is qualified by a 5 kg middle-level and 10 kg bottom-level limit. Capacity for an otherwise unspecified level is not inferred from subtraction.
Tray self-pickup detection is claimed above 99 percent by the manufacturer without an independent accuracy test. Up to 13.5 hours is an operating-endurance claim.
A generic charging footnote appears, but the reviewed table gives no numeric charging duration; no time is inherited from T8, T9 or T10.
T9 carries 40 kg total with a 10 kg per-layer limit; the total is not a per-tray allowance.
Adjustable tray spacing, an accessible touchscreen, independent suspension and shock absorption support restaurant service.

Mapped navigation, obstacle perception and multi-robot dispatch support route coordination. The manufacturer rates up to eighteen hours of operation, with actual endurance dependent on use and settings.
The four-hour charging figure applies from 15 to 100 percent while powered on, using an adapter or charging pile. The page explicitly excludes the charging pile from the supplied package.
T3 uses enclosed automatic doors with foot activation and password access for controlled food delivery; the 180 L cabin is volume, separate from 40 kg total payload.
Triple stereo vision, mapped positioning, a shock-absorbing chassis and coordinated robot dispatch are described for indoor delivery and tray return.
The page supports autonomous elevator use, which requires a compatible installed building integration; elevator support is not proof of operation in every building.
A charge-time interior disinfection light is described by the manufacturer. Its presence does not establish independently verified sterilization, clinical efficacy or medical certification.
Body mass is 71 kg, minimum passage 75 cm and operating endurance up to twelve hours. No numeric charging duration is stated in the reviewed specification table.
S300 uses a lifting platform for 300 kg loads and shelves up to 1200 x 1200 mm; delivery modes include loop, direct, multi-point and transport.
On-device path planning and task execution are described for standalone operation without Wi-Fi/5G or a central control system; this does not establish every fleet feature works offline.

The eight-hour battery claim is explicitly conditioned on operating loads below 100 kg; it does not establish eight hours at the claimed maximum load.
Charging is 2.5 hours from zero to full with the robot powered on. Charging pile, adapter and a claimed fifteen-second battery swap are different replenishment methods.
The minimum passage is printed as 90 cm without rotation but paired with 29.53 inches, approximately 75 cm. The unit disagreement remains unresolved; the metric value is retained with its warning.
A preinstalled OS/app supports deployment. The page describes dual LiDAR, VSLAM and three emergency stops, without establishing independently tested safety performance or certification.

Autonomous charging requires the matching dock and installation; round-the-clock operation includes charging periods rather than unlimited battery endurance.

Power-assisted mapping, automatic environmental labeling and map updates support deployment; the advertised twenty-minute setup for a 3000 m² supermarket depends on site conditions.
Automatic wastewater-tank flushing and suction-path rinsing support maintenance. Twenty-five kilograms of cleaning pressure is not cargo payload.
A 60 Ah LFP battery has mode-dependent lower-bound runtimes of at least four hours scrubbing, eight sweeping and ten dust mopping; these are not a stated maximum endurance.
The page pairs 1.4 m/s with 4.27 ft/s, which are not equivalent. Metric speed is retained with an explicit unit conflict. Theoretical area rates do not establish practical facility productivity.
Marvel combines front dual-side-brush sweeping with rear disc scrubbing for large commercial facilities, supported by 3D LiDAR and surrounding vision.

The 120 Ah LFP battery table separates five-to-seven-hour scrubbing, at least ten-hour sweeping and at least thirteen-hour dust mopping. The overview five-to-ten-hour range lacks those mode qualifications.
Fifty-five kilograms of brush pressure is not payload. Large 80 L/70 L water tanks reduce refill frequency without establishing unattended uptime.
The scrubbing table pairs 3024 m²/h with 21700 ft²/h, approximately 2016 m²/h. The inconsistent unit pair remains visible; other mode rates stay separate.

A power-assisting handle supports manual transport; a stand-on pedal is optional. Wastewater-tank flushing and suction-path rinsing are self-maintenance functions, not proof of a bundled automatic station.

Jobs are taught by physically guiding the arm and using visual tablet tiles. EtherNet/IP, TCP/IP and Modbus support machine integration. Programming simplicity is manufacturer positioning, not a guarantee that every factory task needs no integration or training.

highlights: The manufacturer explicitly names Blaze with 1550 mm including MIG torch. Standard Blaze and long-reach Max are separate named sizes; neither reach is a bare-arm radius without the torch.

The page lists up to 2540 mm/min welding feed, continuous/tack/stitch/weave modes and ±0.1 mm repeatability. Feed is process motion, not a free-motion TCP limit; repeatability is not absolute positioning accuracy or a guaranteed weld-quality result.

Teach-by-touch, drag-and-drop recipes and compatibility with Miller, Lincoln and other welders support integration. Miller Auto-Continuum and Auto Deltaweld 350/500 are selectable source options; amperage, power and source duty cycle are not robot payload or runtime.

An optional synchronized rotary positioning table adds an external axis. The cobot remains seven-axis; the table is not an additional robot. IP61 is stated for the sealed controller and IP41 for the tablet on this page, without certifying a complete MIG installation rating.

The laser page explicitly separates Blaze Laser at 1550 mm including laser torch. The series page calls the larger version Blaze Max Laser; this is the same linked larger-size offering, not a third laser-arm card.

The linked two-size PDF gives up to 2540 mm/min welding feed and ±0.1 mm repeatability. It separately gives 2 m/s maximum position-dependent linear motion and a 0-2+ m/s speed line; the motion-speed discrepancy stays qualified. Feed, free motion and repeatability remain different metrics.

The robot specification states IP61, alongside a separately rated IP61 sealed controller and IP41 tablet. A shared 22 kg/58 lb robot mass is internally inconsistent and not assigned to either size; Miller source mass 64 kg is not the whole robot or cell.

Miller OptX 1 kW is listed for welding; 2 kW adds cleaning. The 2 kW PDF lists 32 A input while LF/Mobile option tables list 20 A; the exact selected-source revision needs confirmation, not a unified electrical requirement. The PDF distinguishes a Class 4 processing laser and Class 2M guide beam.

Teach-by-touch recipes, adjustable weld/cleaning modes and low-heat-input claims describe manufacturer features. Marketing about doubled productivity, any-material welding or no safety equipment is not independently certified. Laser power, source duty cycle and cleaning width are not battery endurance or robot payload.

highlights: The Mobile page explicitly names Blaze Mobile and distinguishes 61-inch standard from 85-inch Max reach; the reviewed size corresponds to 1550 mm including torch. The heavy rolling frame has locking wheels and is not described as autonomous navigation.
Teach-by-touch and drag-and-drop recipes control up to 2540 mm/min welding feed, with ±0.1 mm repeatability. Neither value is a driving speed, autonomous docking accuracy or payload rating.

MIG or laser sources are selectable; the page offers the Auto-Continuum 350 configuration with an option to exclude the welder. A complete source, process tools and electrical requirement are order dependent, not universal included equipment.

The 1 kW OptX option lists welding; 2 kW lists welding and cleaning. Its 64 kg source mass, source current, average/peak laser power and duty-cycle ratings do not establish the mass, payload, endurance or safety certification of the complete Mobile system.

The August 2026 sheet specifies 150 kg total capacity including payload, attachments and cart where fitted,107 kg chassis mass and 740 x 550 x 308 mm dimensions. The integrated lift has 62 mm stroke and 150 kg capacity; stroke is not maximum fork height.

Maximum travel speed is 2.0 m/s, docking approach 0.3 m/s and turning is in place. Minimum aisles are 1099 mm one-way/1975 mm two-way without payload. A turn-in-place description is not a zero-clearance swept-envelope guarantee.

Standard translational docking is±10 mm in x/y; the separately sold HADS upgrade lists±5 mm. Angular/repeatability notation is not normalized from the source. Docking approach speed, docking accuracy and general navigation accuracy are different quantities.

Runtime is six hours from 90% to 10% state of charge; charging is 18 minutes from 10% to 90%. The 35 Ah/26.4 V pack,98 A maximum charge rate and 10,000 full-cycle battery-life claim do not establish ten-thousand-hour endurance or a full 0–100% charging duration.

The sheet distinguishes 13 mm floor obstacles from 6 mm ground clearance, statesIP20 and 20–40°C ambient operation. Forward 3D perception, rearToF sensing, cart detection and laser scanning support the workflow. Compliance and collision-resilience statements remain manufacturer claims, not independently reviewed site safety.

OTTO Carts,98 A autonomous/25 A manual chargers and HADS are listed as separately sold accessories. Fleet Manager offers battery-aware dispatch, opportunity charging, traffic coordination and Open API/OPC-UA integration; software/attachment selection and installation remain project dependent.

The September 2026 OTTO 600 sheet gives 600 kg total including an attachment if fitted,250 kg mass and 1050 x 700 x 320 mm body dimensions. Rated load is not the model number interpreted as net freight after adding accessories.

Maximum travel speed is 1.4 m/s and docking approach 0.3 m/s. The source specifies 1575 mm one-way; no payload, in-place turning,16 mm ground clearance and 4 mm floor obstacles. Clearance is not an obstacle-height or payload-included aisle guarantee.

The 21 Ah/48 V energy system lists 30-minute charging from 10% to 90% and 6,000 full charge cycles. It does not state hours-per-charge runtime; no endurance is inferred from cycle life or another OTTO model.

The named DTG3 specification lists 8.5 kg in air, 279 x 325 x 258 mm body dimensions in length × width × height order, and 200 m depth rating. Cases, controllers, tether reels and tool assemblies are separate.

Die-cast aluminum body, acrylic window and magnetically coupled/sealed drives. The camera specification describes enhanced 4K video, 8 MP stills and 270° total range of view; this is not an extra body degree of freedom.

The DTG3 page compares current ROV models. Its PHOTON card says 215° camera rotation, while PHOTON structured Product/FAQ data says 200°. That disagreement belongs to PHOTON and is not a second DTG3 camera range.

No exact per-charge endurance, full-charge duration, payload, complete-robot IP class or first hardware-release year is established by this reviewed product page. Portable power and batteries do not supply numeric endurance by inference.

The named PHOTON specification lists 11.8 kg in air, 481 x 332 x 228 mm body dimensions in length × width × height order, and 120 m depth rating. Cases, controllers, tether reels and tool assemblies are separate.

Six independently controlled, fully reversible thrusters and 19.2 VDC power. The page specifies enhanced 4K video and 8 MP stills. The tether can be up to 300 m; tether length is not the 120 m depth rating.

The BASE and EXPERT offers are packages of PHOTON. The embedded FAQ describes EXPERT as adding a grabber, longer tether and a second battery; battery count does not establish per-charge operating hours.
Camera rotation is inconsistent across source layers: PHOTON embedded Product/FAQ data says 200°, while the DTG3 page comparison card says 215°. No silently reconciled camera rotation is selected.

No exact per-charge endurance, full-charge duration, payload, complete-robot IP class or first hardware-release year is established by this reviewed product page. Portable power and batteries do not supply numeric endurance by inference.

highlights: The named PIVOT specification lists 23.6 kg in air, 576 x 360 x 310 mm body dimensions in length × width × height order, and 305 m depth rating. Cases, controllers, tether reels and tool assemblies are separate.

Six independently controlled, fully reversible thrusters and 19.2 VDC power. Enhanced 4K video and 8 MP stills are specified. USBL, DVL and sonar support depends on package and add-ons; no universal numeric positioning tolerance is established.

The page distinguishes SMART, EXPERT, RECON and NAV packages: SMART has one battery set and 100 m tether; EXPERT and RECON have two sets and 150 m; NAV has two sets and 300 m. EXPERT and NAV list a grabber, while SMART and RECON do not. Battery sets do not establish a continuous runtime.
The embedded FAQ describes a 97° tilting shelf separately from 220° camera rotation. Accessories and imaging angles are not arm joint counts or guaranteed positioning accuracy.

No exact per-charge endurance, full-charge duration, payload, complete-robot IP class or first hardware-release year is established by this reviewed product page. Portable power and batteries do not supply numeric endurance by inference.

The named REVOLUTION specification lists 33 kg in air, 717 x 440 x 235 mm body dimensions in length × width × height order, and 305 m depth rating. Cases, controllers, tether reels and tool assemblies are separate.

The electrical specification lists 19.2 VDC, 18 Ah LiFePO4. Copper tether options up to 300 m and fiber options up to 2 km are not dive-depth or battery-runtime figures. Enhanced 4K video and 8 MP stills are specified.

BASE, RECON and NAV are packages. The embedded FAQ associates RECON with ROV GPS, DVL and SensorPod+, and NAV with USBL, DVL and SensorPod+. Visible package cards list a grabber; external manipulators remain add-ons.

The embedded FAQ describes a 260° rotating camera head and optional rotating sonar. BRIDGE station keeping, dead reckoning and mission planning require the documented equipment; the feature names do not establish universal autonomy or an exact navigation tolerance.

No exact per-charge endurance, full-charge duration, payload, complete-robot IP class or first hardware-release year is established by this reviewed product page. Portable power and batteries do not supply numeric endurance by inference.

The named SPECTRA specification lists 38 kg in air, 790 x 586 x 296 mm body dimensions in length × width × height order, and 1000 m depth rating. Cases, controllers, tether reels and tool assemblies are separate.
Seven thrusters comprise four vectored and three vertical units. The stated 40 kg thrust force is not payload. Dual 4K video and 12 MP stills accompany two 150,000-lumen lights, 300,000 lumens total.

Visible specifications list 3.5 knots forward and 2.3 knots lateral, but embedded Product JSON-LD describes 4 knots maximum. The source conflict remains explicit. Maximum current-operation wording is not an independently tested capability.

Real-time Sonar SLAM is explicitly enabled with 3D sonar only. The 300 m standard fiber tether and additional kilometer options are separate from the 1000 m depth rating; sonar integration is not universally included.

Direct topside power is specified at 100–260 VAC, 50–60 Hz and 7200 W maximum draw, with 48 V nominal onboard and 1000 W accessory-port power. Accessory watts are not payload. Under-30-minute modular servicing is not a charge time or battery duration.

MAG uses magnetic wheels on ferrous surfaces, magnetically coupled final drives and a 19.2 V lithium battery system. The product page advertises enhanced 4K cameras and sonar integration; tooling and sonar configuration require confirmation.

The general specification gives 16.6 kg, 710 mm length, 406 mm width and 228 mm height, with 50 m depth rating. Width is also labeled 13 inches, inconsistent with 406 mm; the source disagreement is retained.
The page labels 360° as turn radius. An angle is not a length, so no numeric turning radius or zero-clearance guarantee is selected.

The IP68 claim is under Tether Reel, not the robot. The 150 kg minimum tether breaking strength is not crawler payload. Tether options of 50–400 m and the standard 75 m reel are distinct from 50 m dive depth.
Incline, roll, leak and camera-pan/tilt sensors do not establish numeric navigation accuracy. Exact battery endurance and full-charge duration are not documented on the reviewed page.
The VAC family page lists 15 kg, 710 × 406 × 228 mm, 50 m submersion depth, 12 m/min speed and rubber 2WD. It pairs 406 mm width with 13 inches; that unresolved unit conflict remains visible.

The shop package states up to eight hours on battery and hybrid trickle charging during operation. This is not a full-charge duration, nor a guarantee for maximum speed, cleaning load or indefinite battery-only operation.

The two-inch vacuum intakes connect to a hose and submersible pump. The shop explicitly excludes the hose and pump. The articulated head has separate 20° raise and tilt travel, which is not a manipulator joint count.

Camera revision is unresolved: the visible family specification says enhanced 4K, while the shop embedded electrical table says 1080p main-camera video with 8 MP sensor data. Neither image pixels nor the family headline reconcile the delivered video mode.

The stated zero-millimeter turning radius does not establish zero surrounding clearance. IP68 belongs to the tether reel, and 150 kg tether strength is not crawler payload. The shop URL containing XL and 18-inch is not evidence of a separate VAC XL model.
